findings.reason: without a case that makes the namings reader refuse, a worker can pass every stated assertion while returning a different held map on the path the section explicitly promises to preserve.
findings.text: §61's deliverable states that "the path taken when the namings reader refuses (`_run_file_rows`, near line 2075) still returns the same answer", but the done-when enumerates only the ordinary path (a fixture of 500 records, named and unnamed trees, a call count and a reference map), so no case drives `_run_namings` to return `None`. That is the one path where the screen is dropped entirely and every row becomes a candidate, which is precisely where a bounded rewrite is most likely to change the answer — the flagging comment at `reckon/crew/obligations.py:2266-2273` records that a refused reader must never cost a duty.

findings.reason: the base/head logs and the red-arm log are the whole of these two nodes' evidence; unnamed, they land wherever the worker's run directory happens to be and no later reader can open them from the plan.
findings.text: neither §61 nor §62 names where its gate logs or its negative-control log live: both stop at "Each log names its revision, tree and literal command, and ends in `EXIT=`", and neither write-path list carries a `docs/evidence/fragments/a-read-answers-inside-its-deadline/…` target, while §58 and §59 in the same plan do. The only concrete evidence path either section gives is §61's profile log at `~/.cache/reckon-held-fallback/probe-20261109.log`, a cache directory rather than a landed record.

rubric_items.wiring: pass — §61 and §62 write `reckon/crew/obligations.py`, `reckon/crew/routing.py` and `reckon/flight.py`, none of which another open section of this plan writes (§44 writes `recovery_watch.py`, §58 writes `node.py`, §59 writes `serve.py`), and no live run declares any of the three as a write path; the sections they cite as prior bounds (§21, §23) are done, and §62's use of §61 is evidence reuse from an existing probe, not an output dependency.
